subject_line: Walking with your father to the desert prison in Under a Future Sky
email_body:
Dear Brynn,
Under a Future Sky starts from a journey with your father to the desert prison where your grandparents met, and its letters and lyric correspondences read like a way of talking across generations rather than only remembering them.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how the epistolary form came about: did writing to ghosts and family change what you could say about the incarceration, and how does it connect to the Yonsei Memory Project?

subject_line: Shedding what we were sold in What to Wear Out
email_body:
Dear Jen,
What to Wear Out is framed by a sequence written through the COVID-19 pandemic, with a speaker moving from a youth shaped by consumerism and patriarchy toward a midlife effort to shed those constraints.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how the pandemic sequence came to frame the book, and how it felt to launch a debut collection at Binghamton, where you studied and now help direct creative writing.

subject_line: Yunus Turabi and Hajj Saeed in Then the Fish Swallowed Him
email_body:
Dear Amir,
In Then the Fish Swallowed Him, Yunus Turabi is an ordinary Tehran bus driver whose life tips over after a union strike, and much of the novel's pressure comes from his long cat-and-mouse with the interrogator Hajj Saeed in Evin.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you built that interrogation room on the page, and what changed for you in moving from Persian to English as a novelist.

book_title: Frida Kahlo and My Left Leg
subject_line: Seeing yourself in Kahlo in Frida Kahlo and My Left Leg
email_body:
Dear Emily,
Frida Kahlo and My Left Leg moves through fourteen loosely linked essays in which you look at Kahlo through your own experience of disability, and it pushes back against the easy, self-serving readings of her body that so many admirers repeat.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you chose the essay form over a single narrative, and what it was like to write against the popular image of an artist you also love.

subject_line: The lockdown poems of If Only There Were Stations of the Air
email_body:
Dear Judy,
Much of If Only There Were Stations of the Air was written during the Covid lockdowns, and it follows Groaning and Singing, where memoir poems about growing up in a New York tenement became a way of rescuing the beloved dead.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how the isolation of those months changed the way memory works in the new poems, and how a New York tenement childhood and your life in Riverside meet on the page.

subject_line: Chioma's doorstep in After the Rain
email_body:
Dear John,
After the Rain, your adaptation of Nnedi Okorafor's story "On the Road" with David Brame, opens with Chioma answering a knock to find a boy with a terrible head wound, and it launched the Megascope imprint you curate at Abrams ComicArts.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask what adapting Octavia Butler taught you that shaped your approach to Okorafor's story, and what Megascope is trying to make room for.

subject_line: Interviewing your mother before writing Miss Burma
email_body:
Dear Charmaine,
In your Lit Hub essay you describe interviewing your mother years before writing Miss Burma, and her reluctance to revisit parts of her past. The novel follows Benny, Khin and their daughter Louisa through Burma's modern history and the Karen resistance.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you moved from those interviews, pieced together almost journalistically, to the freedom of fiction, and what it meant to see Karen readers in the US respond to the book.

subject_line: Dogs, ghosts and kōans in Separation Anxiety
email_body:
Dear Janice,
Separation Anxiety moves through the approaching deaths of the speaker's dogs and memories of a mother who has died, in short untitled poems that one reviewer compared to kōans on postcards. It reads very differently from the long, trance-like sentences of Imagine a Death, though both circle grief.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you decide whether grief calls for the long sentence or the short fragment, and where interspecies communication fits into that.

subject_line: Dr. Parkman's disappearance in Blood & Ivy
email_body:
Dear Paul,
Blood & Ivy reconstructs the 1849 disappearance of Dr. George Parkman in Boston and the discovery of his remains in John Webster's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, drawing on newspaper accounts, letters, journals and court transcripts. Reviewers kept noting how much eyewitness material you were able to bring in.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you find the story inside an archive like that, and how you teach that kind of research-driven nonfiction to students at Portland State.

subject_line: Rooms instead of chapters in Wolf Bells
email_body:
Dear Leni,
In Wolf Bells, the house above the river run by Caz, a former punk singer who never wanted to be responsible for anyone, is upended when Nola and her cousin James arrive after running from Child Protective Services. Each scene is labeled with the room it happens in rather than a chapter title.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask where that room-by-room structure came from, and what drew you to this shared household.

subject_line: Reworking the epic in What Noise Against the Cane
email_body:
Dear Desiree,
What Noise Against the Cane opens by reworking the epic as an oceanic story of bondage and liberation during the Haitian Revolution, then moves into the contemporary Black diaspora and its myths of home, belief, nation and womanhood. Carl Phillips wrote that the poems argue for hope and faith equally.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask why the epic felt like the right form to begin with, and how that opening sequence shaped the shorter poems that follow it.

subject_line: Barbara's unauthorized memoir in Night Night Fawn
email_body:
Dear Jordy,
Night Night Fawn gives the narration to Barbara Rosenberg, dying in a rent-controlled Manhattan apartment and writing her life story while her estranged trans child appears to be turning into a large, ragged bird, and she cannot tell whether that is real, hallucination or punishment. BookBrowse called it part novel, part someone's mother's unauthorized memoir.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask what it meant to hand the voice to the mother, and how satire helped you write about family friction.

subject_line: The residents' monologues in Shale Play
email_body:
Dear Julia,
Shale Play sets your poems beside Steven Rubin's photographs of the towns, farms and forests of Appalachian Pennsylvania in the Marcellus Shale, and a reviewer in Mennonite Writing singled out the monologues of local residents as its most compelling poems.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you gathered those voices, how working alongside a photographer changed what the poems needed to do, and whether the project has altered how you approach documentary poetry with students at Penn State.

email_body:
Dear Cynthia,
Futureless Languages takes its frame from languages that express the future in the present tense, and its middle section turns to prose poems about memory and permanence. For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how the two books talk to each other, and why the prose poem felt right for the sequence at the book's centre.

subject_line: From fifty flash fictions to As Is
email_body:
Dear Nathan,
Your flash collection The Origin of Doubt gathered fifty very short fictions and was a Lambda Literary Award finalist, and your newer book, As Is: Essays on a Queer Life, turns to the essay. I'm curious about that movement from compressed invented stories to personal nonfiction.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask what the essay allowed you to say that flash fiction didn't, and how teaching creative writing at Stockton has shaped the way you think about brevity.

subject_line: House-sitting for Uncle Lech in The Made-Up Man
email_body:
Dear Joe,
In The Made-Up Man, Stanley agrees to house-sit his Uncle Lech's Prague apartment for three days without knowing he is about to become the star of one of Lech's immersive performance pieces. One review called it part noir, part bildungsroman, part psychological thriller, which sums up how hard it is to pin down.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask what drew you to performance art as the engine of a novel, and how you balanced its comedy against its sense of menace.

subject_line: Unravelling a diagnosis in A Fish Growing Lungs
email_body:
Dear Alysia,
A Fish Growing Lungs traces, in linked essays, a bipolar I diagnosis at eighteen, the discovery seven years later that it was a misdiagnosis, and the withdrawal and recovery that followed. In your Rumpus Book Club chat you mentioned that the collection came together partly because you needed an MFA thesis.
For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you chose the linked-essay form for a story about identity coming apart and back together, and how teaching has changed your writing since.
